items.body:
Anthropic手握超2300亿美元资金，CEO却还想借钱研发AI

Anthropic 刚完成史上最大规模的 IPO。根据最终招股书，以 9 月底的财务数据为基础，计入上市募资及 260 亿美元配套私募后，公司预计拥有约 2324 亿美元现金及短期投资。

这笔巨款还远远覆盖不了 Anthropic 的算力野心。公司已签下约 9009 亿美元的长期算力及基础设施合同，其中约 707 亿美元预计在未来 12 个月内到期。

Anthropic 甚至开始提前锁定发电设备。今年 9 月，公司签下约 34 亿美元的协议，向得州供应商 OnePWR 预订总计 1.7 吉瓦的天然气发电机组，以及配套的工程建设资源，为未来的数据中心供电。

上市当天，CEO Dario Amodei 在 CNBC 采访中表示，9000 亿美元的算力承诺分散在未来多年。考虑到公司现有的现金和收入规模，实际负担没有数字看起来那么夸张。

他还希望 Anthropic 未来获得投资级信用评级，进一步通过发行债券融资。即使已经筹集超过千亿美元，公司仍准备继续借钱扩张算力。

Amodei 同日在上市致辞中重申，Anthropic 会根据安全需要放慢 AI 模型的训练和发布，无论需要多长时间，都不会向商业或政治压力妥协。

items.body:
Anthropic上市未能缓解AI相关忧虑，亚洲芯片股遭遇抛售

11 月 20 日，尽管 Anthropic 成功上市，但亚洲芯片相关股票周五仍重现跌势。这表明，过去数月不断累积的、针对 AI 相关投资的担忧，依然主导着投资者的情绪。

在日本，芯片测试设备制造商爱德万测试股价一度大跌 12%，科技投资巨头软银集团在东京股市重挫 17%，拖累日经 225 指数跌至 4 月以来的最低水平。在韩国，SK 海力士和三星电子的跌幅均超过 6%。即便是在中国台湾——当地为稳定股市已收紧了卖空限制——相关股票也遭到抛售，台积电和联发科股价均出现下滑。AI 行业近期频频出现令其长期前景蒙上阴影的动态。

美国中期选举后的监管风险，以及英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋突然离职的消息，加剧了市场对于企业巨额支出及其变现前景的担忧。盛宝金融首席投资策略师 Charu Chanana 表示：「AI 相关投资此前就已面临诸多质疑，例如基础设施支出是否过度、是否存在循环融资，以及投资回报能否覆盖投入成本。

Anthropic 的成功上市并未解答这些疑问。相反，它吸引了更多资本涌入前沿 AI 模型领域——而这一领域竞争异常激烈，定价权正在减弱，盈利能力也依然充满不确定性。」

items.body:
谷歌Gemini Mac版上线“电脑操控”功能

谷歌日前为macOS版Gemini应用推出全新的“电脑操控”（Computer Use）功能，允许AI直接操作用户电脑，跨本地文件、桌面应用和网页执行多步骤任务。目前，该功能正面向美国地区的英语用户逐步开放。

据谷歌公司介绍，新功能使Gemini不再局限于对话和内容生成，而是能够直接参与电脑操作，帮助用户完成复杂工作流程。例如，Gemini可以协助填写在线表单、制作演示文稿、处理创意工作，以及完成商品上架销售等任务。在权限管理方面，用户可以自主决定允许Gemini访问哪些应用程序。执行任务时，Gemini会在后台窗口中运行，并通过聊天界面内的实时预览窗口展示操作过程。

—— 凤凰网科技、The Verge

苹果数据“后门”风波再起 英国政府被迫承认秘密命令

英国法院裁定，英国政府必须承认曾向苹果公司发出秘密命令，该命令要求苹果允许政府获取经过加密的用户数据。这一裁决为英国内政部与这家美国科技巨头围绕隐私和安全问题展开公开法律交锋铺平了道路。

items.body:
做空机构质疑 AMD 涉华业务存在出口管制风险

做空机构 Hunterbrook 发布 AMD 做空报告，质疑公司涉华业务可能存在美国出口管制合规风险。报告称，中国服务器厂商浪潮信息 2025 年被美国列入实体清单后，相关服务器仍持续发布包含 AMD 新版本固件的更新，最近一次更新于今年 10 月 19 日。

此外，报告发现，三家关联服务器厂商发布的固件与浪潮版本高度相似，相似度最高达 99.94%，质疑相关技术是否通过关联企业流转，涉及受限制实体。Hunterbrook 尚未证实 AMD 存在违规行为，但认为公司可能面临潜在合规风险。受此消息影响，AMD 股价盘中一度下跌超过 10%。

items.summary: Hebbia tested GPT-6 Astra for financial research. Its prerelease evaluations found gains in source coverage, citation relevance, and presentation quality.
items.body:

Hebbia sees gains in financial research in tests of GPT‑6 Astra.

Before a banker can recommend an acquisition to their client, they need to make sense of financial statements, customer contracts and management presentations. Hebbia’s Matrix helps bring that research together, linking answers to the documents behind them.

Hebbia tested OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra to improve two parts of that work: finding the sources a question requires and building a presentation that follows the banker’s brief.

“We’ve been strong partners with OpenAI over the course of Hebbia’s lifetime, and the leaps GPT-6 Astra has made in terms of quality outputs and accuracy have truly been surprising. GPT-6 Astra shines compared to any other model we’ve tested before on these two fronts.”

—Kavita Anand, Member of Technical Staff, Product, Hebbia

It could work like this: a banker is helping their client assess a strategic acquisition of an industrial-software company, with roughly 2,000 files to review. What makes its revenue durable? How does it compare with peers? In Hebbia’s hypothetical example, the banker could load the data room into Matrix and examine customer concentration, contract terms and churn in cited cells. Matrix could bring in peer filings and industry news to help develop the deal thesis, then turn that research into a diligence summary and valuation deck in the firm’s template.

In that workflow, GPT‑6 Astra selects documents or Matrix cells to support an answer, then turns the analysis into native PowerPoint slides that follow the user’s structure and guidelines.

“Traceability is really important to our users because they’re basing millions of dollars of decisions on what the AI actually comes back with,” Kavita says. “Citations help with traceability as well as giving users confidence that the AI found the right answer.”

In Hebbia’s tests, GPT‑6 Astra combined broader source coverage with highly relevant citations. It scored 13.6 percentage points above the best alternative tested on citing the required types of sources, while 99.5% of the excerpts it cited were relevant to the question.

Hebbia tested a prerelease build in August-September 2026, using the same financial research cases and grading criteria for each model. Domain experts wrote or audited the criteria against source documents.

“When you’re looking at a data room with thousands of documents, that’s extremely important. Even a single percentage-point gain can yield a lot of marginal benefit,” Kavita says.

A presentation also has to look like work the banker would send to a client.

“I don’t want to create a deck and send that to my partner that looks like AI made it,” Kavita says. “I want it to be made in my firm’s branding, and I want it to look like a human-made slide.”

GPT‑6 Astra led on both following the brief and presentation quality. In Hebbia’s tests, it met 97.9% of the applicable presentation requirements, putting it 14.4 percentage points ahead of the best alternative tested on that measure. Other models traded off polish and adherence to the brief; GPT‑6 Astra ranked first on both.

“In the past, we’ve seen models that really shine on one or the other of these dimensions where they’re really good at craft, but the instruction following and adhering to guidelines is not strong, or vice versa. GPT‑6 Astra is the first model we’ve seen where it’s number one on both of those fronts,” Kavita says.

In Hebbia, users can open a citation to see the underlying document and highlighted passage; slide footnotes lead back to the source material, too. A review could be as specific as checking a customer-concentration figure against the source table and correcting the reporting period before the deck goes to the investment committee.

Hebbia wants bankers to spend less time reformatting decks and checking sources, and more time assessing a deal. Kavita describes what a better first draft could make possible:

“What’s amazing about GPT-6 Astra is its ability to create really precise outputs and artifacts that adhere to user guidelines. You can imagine the hours this will save professionals when you get a deck that is closer to your final output. The overnighters that you have to pull get reduced to a few minutes of reviewing GPT-6 Astra’s output.”

—Kavita Anand, Member of Technical Staff, Product, Hebbia

Kavita sees a future role for agents that monitor information in the background and surface signals for finance professionals to assess.

“Imagine getting an important signal a few hours before your competitors,” she says. “You can get started thinking about it and see and process more opportunities that a human is not manually hunting. It can unlock a lot of value for our users.”

Hebbia wants to build on these results to help finance professionals assess deals with research they can trace back to its sources.

items.title: Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates?
items.summary: MedChemBench evaluates how well AI models interpret molecular structures, reason from experimental evidence, and select compounds in early drug discovery.
items.body:
November 20, 2026

ResearchReleaseScience

Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next.

Read the paper(opens in a new window)

00:00

We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines.

One of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. For AI to help, it needs to connect changes in molecular structure with experimental evidence and reason about what compounds are worth pursuing.

MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model.

MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings.

The benchmark evaluates four components:

• Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided.

• Scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another.

• Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements.

• Property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties.

One MedChemBench problem draws on research into inhibitors of PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. The model receives molecular structures and results from earlier experiments. It must predict how three related compounds will behave: how strongly they block PRMT5 in cells, how readily they cross a cell barrier, and how quickly liver enzymes break them down in a laboratory assay.

Later experiments, withheld from the model, showed a tradeoff. Compound 23 blocked PRMT5 in cells at a lower concentration, while compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay.

Predicting these properties together tests whether a model can connect molecular structures with several aspects of compound behavior. This reflects a central challenge in medicinal chemistry: stronger activity against a target does not necessarily come with better permeability or slower breakdown.

The benchmark checks whether the model reconstructs the molecular structures correctly and how closely its predictions match experimental measurements. Predictions receive partial credit based on their closeness to the measured values. Measurements already supplied in the prompt must also be reproduced correctly.

Before a model can reason about a compound’s properties, it needs to identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connections, ring structures, and stereochemistry.

MedChemBench tests whether models preserve this information when reconstructing molecules from the drawings and chemical groups provided.

One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At the highest reasoning setting shared by all eleven models (xhigh), GPT‑6 Astra reconstructed this compound correctly in all ten responses. GPT‑5.6 Sol and GPT‑5.6 Luna failed across all ten responses.

In the illustrated answers, GPT‑5.6 Sol produced a 15-atom ring, while GPT‑5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected fragments.

These errors change the identity of the molecule being analyzed. This example tests a foundation of medicinal chemistry reasoning: whether the model can accurately represent the compound before interpreting its behavior.

Figure 1. The same input, different molecules

While measuring the benchmark for structure components, Astra earned 95.4% of the available credit at xhigh. This result shows strong performance on reconstructing the molecular structures supplied in the tasks.

We evaluated eleven GPT models at different reasoning-effort settings. Across the full benchmark, Astra earned 83.3% of the available credit at the shared xhigh setting, compared with 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT‑6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. At max effort, GPT‑6 Astra reached 83.8%. Higher reasoning settings improved scores, while large differences between models remained. The figure below plots performance against output tokens.

Figure 2. Performance versus token usage

The component results separate four abilities: reconstructing molecules, explaining findings, selecting compounds, and predicting measurements. This shows where models are strongest and where errors remain.

Figure 3. Component performance versus token usage

Astra’s clearest strengths were in reconstructing molecular structures and explaining the scientific evidence. In selected reasoning examples from our preprint, Astra correctly identified structural changes and weighed their possible effects on protein binding, absorption, and metabolism.

Where selection and prediction remain difficult, Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh, but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. These categories use different tasks and scoring rules, but the results show substantial room to improve predictions and compound choices.

These results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out, and each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments. While the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery, its results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain. We believe MedChemBench will support continued progress and look forward to sharing updates as our models advance to serve the field.

items.title: How we’re putting one of quantum mechanics’ deepest features to the test at scale.
items.summary: Google Quantum AI research proves contextuality powers quantum algorithms at scale. See how our processor beat classical limits. Get the details.
items.body:
How we’re putting one of quantum mechanics’ deepest features to the test at scale.

Nov 19, 2026

Today, in new research published on the cover of Science, Google Quantum AI demonstrated that contextuality — a quantum property scientists believe powers certain quantum algorithms — survives at scale on our quantum processor.

What gives quantum computers their unique power? While entanglement usually gets the spotlight, theory suggests that a deeper quantum property called contextuality may power certain quantum algorithms. In simple terms, contextuality means a system’s properties aren’t fixed in advance; what you measure depends on which other compatible measurements you make alongside it.

Until recently, this effect had mostly been shown in small systems of just a few particles. Our paper in Science now demonstrates this at scale on our quantum processor. Using it, our qubits won a well-known coordination game 98.3% of the time, beating the 88.9% classical limit, and outperformed constrained classical strategies in tasks spanning up to 105 qubits.

These tests also serve as a sensitive new method to catch subtle hardware errors, helping pave the way for real-world applications like chemistry and materials science. Read the full Google Research blog post to learn more.

Tool Retrieval is now in preview in the Gemini Interactions API. Load tool parameter schemas on demand instead of sending your full tool library in every prompt,designed to reduce input tokens and keep tool selection accurate as your agent scales.

Lucia Loher

Product Manager, Gemini API

Nora Kassner

Research Scientist, Google DeepMind

We are launching Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API to help your agents manage large tool libraries more efficiently. By loading parameter schemas only when needed, you reduce latency and input token costs for complex tasks. You can try this feature today in the Interactions API by adding a tool_search tool and setting defer_loading to true in your requests.

• This feature reduces input token counts and latency by loading parameter schemas only when needed.

• You can enable this by adding a tool search and setting defer loading to true.

We are introducing Tool Retrieval to help developers manage large collections of software tools more efficiently. Instead of loading every tool at once, your agent now keeps a library on standby and only pulls in the specific details it needs for a task. This reduces data usage, speeds up performance, and improves accuracy. You can start using this feature today with our latest Gemini models to build more capable and responsive applications.

Explore other styles:

Today we're launching Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API, available in preview in the Interactions API.

When an agent connects to dozens or even hundreds of tools, sending every full parameter schema on every request adds up fast. It inflates input token counts, adds latency, and lowers tool-selection accuracy as the candidate list grows. Tool Retrieval lets your agent keep its full tool library on standby and load parameter schemas only when the current task needs them.

How it works

To turn on Tool Retrieval, add a tool_search tool to your request and set defer_loading: true on the tools you want to hold back. The model still sees the name and description of every deferred tool, so it knows what's available, but the parameter schemas stay out of context. When the model needs a tool, it asks for it by name, the API loads the full schema, and the model calls the function, all inside the same request.

from google import genai

client = genai.Client()

tools = [
   {"type": "tool_search"},
   {
       "type": "function",
       "name": "issue_refund",
       "description": "Refund an order to the original payment method.",
       "defer_loading": True,
       "parameters": {
           "type": "object",
           "properties": {
               "order_id": {"type": "string"},
               "amount": {"type": "number"},
           },
           "required": ["order_id", "amount"],
       },
   },
   # ... 50+ other deferred functions (leave frequent tools undeferred)
]

interaction = client.interactions.create(
   model="gemini-4-hydrogen",
   input="Order A-1042 arrived damaged. Please refund 40 dollars.",
   tools=tools,
)

Inside that single API call, the model searches for issue_refund, the API loads its schema, and the model emits the function_call. All three steps appear in interaction.steps, making it easy to inspect which tools the model considered when debugging tool names or descriptions:

"steps": [
 {
   "type": "tool_search_call",
   "id": "tsc_7f2a",
   "arguments": {"function_names": ["issue_refund"]},
   "signature": "..."
 },
 {
   "type": "tool_search_result",
   "call_id": "tsc_7f2a",
   "result": [{"type": "function", "name": "issue_refund", "parameters": {...}}],
   "signature": "..."
 },
 {
   "type": "function_call",
   "id": "fc_91c3",
   "name": "issue_refund",
   "arguments": {"order_id": "A-1042", "amount": 40}
 }
]

From here it's normal function calling: your code runs the refund and sends back a function_result.

There's no index to build or host. Gemini runs the search on the server, so the only changes to your code are the new tool and a flag on the tools you want to defer. You can keep your most-used tools loaded up front and defer the long tail.

Tool Retrieval also plays well with prefix caching. Deferred schemas stay out of the start of the prompt, and the schemas the model loads are added later in the conversation, so the cached prefix stays the same from turn to turn.

Tool Retrieval also works with remote MCP servers in the Gemini API. Set defer_loading: true on an mcp_server tool and every tool that server exposes is loaded on demand, so you can connect a large server without listing its tools one by one.

How client-side retrieval works

If you maintain your own tool registry, embedding index, or per-user permission filter, declare the tool_search with "execution": "client" and define your search parameters. Client-side retrieval adds one round trip per search, because your app runs the lookup. Tools do not need to be declared upfront, so you can also expose new tools mid-conversation when a user connects an integration:

tools = [{
    "type": "tool_search",
    "execution": "client",
    "name": "search_tools",
    "description": "Search the internal tool registry for functions.",
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["query"],
    },
}]

# When the model emits a function_call for "search_tools",
# return matching {"type": "function", ...} schemas in function_result:
followup = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-4-hydrogen",
    previous_interaction_id=interaction.id,
    tools=tools,
    input=[{
        "type": "function_result",
        "name": "search_tools",
        "call_id": step.id,
        "result": my_registry.search(**step.arguments),
    }],
)

How pricing and supported models work

Tool Retrieval has no separate charge. Input and output tokens are billed at the standard rates for the model you call. Turning on tool_search adds a small, fixed block of input tokens, and each schema the model loads is billed as input for the rest of the conversation, the same as a tool declared up front. You save tokens when the schemas you never load outweigh the ones you do, which is the usual case for large libraries. Measure it against your own traffic.

Tool Retrieval works with Gemini 3.6 and later models, including all Gemini 4 models, in the Interactions API.

A smarter way to track and buy clean energy

Granular certificates are a next-generation tool to ensure more accurate, impactful clean energy buying.

Jenna Stauffer

Head of Strategic Priorities, Climate Operations

We are advancing Granular Certificates to track clean energy by hour and location, providing clear pricing signals that encourage smarter grid management. These tools help you match electricity use with local clean energy production, supporting a more stable power system. You can watch our new video to learn how these certificates help developers, energy asset owners, and the grid.

Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

• We use Granular Certificates to track clean energy supply by specific hour and geographic location.

• Trading volume in the U.S. Mid-Atlantic region increased 437% during our recent monthly spot auctions.

• Our support for the Registry Acceleration Fund helps organizations verify and track hourly energy data.

• These certificates provide new revenue streams for battery storage operators and improve grid stability overall.

• We reduced our Scope 2 emissions by 3% while managing a 37% increase in electricity load.

Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

We are using new tools called Granular Certificates to track clean energy by the hour and location. These certificates help us match our electricity use with local solar or wind power, even when the sun is not shining. By creating clear price signals, this system encourages companies to build more batteries and clean energy projects where they are needed most. This helps us manage our power use and supports a cleaner, more stable energy grid.

Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

Granular Certificates (GCs) are next-generation clean energy instruments. They precisely track supply by hour and location, helping companies match their electricity load with local clean energy. Their hourly pricing signals encourage the development of clean generation and energy storage when and where it is needed most.

These instruments can incentivize improved grid management, and they can help accelerate the deployment of advanced clean technologies, leading to a cleaner, more stable power system. But like any nascent solution, the foundational building blocks need to be in place first.

We first started piloting GCs in 2021 and, in just five years, they’ve transitioned from early concept to real-world certificates, traded on specific hours. We’re continuing to take actions to accelerate both our own procurement and the global GC ecosystem.

Here are three key ways the GC ecosystem advanced this year:

1. The GC marketplace is growing.

Marketplaces are critical because they establish transparent hourly pricing signals and help simplify processes for those new to hourly procurement. LevelTen, in partnership with the Granular Certificate Trading Alliance (GCTA) and the Intercontinental Exchange, launched the Granular Certificate Marketplace in the U.S. Mid-Atlantic grid region PJM in October 2025. Since that first auction, trading volume has increased 437% in just one year, with Google participating in every monthly spot auction.

This increased trading volume generates clear pricing signals, with higher premiums occurring during evening hours. By demonstrating when buyers need clean energy most, GCs can incentivize suppliers to operate or build clean energy to meet this demand.

2. Global registries help with tracking and verification.

Almost every corporate clean energy buyer uses registries, which track and verify their clean energy purchases via instruments like monthly or annual energy attribute certificates (EACs). Registries help also ensure EACs are not double counted, supporting unique clean energy claims. However, until recently, the vast majority of registries didn’t have the technical capabilities to accommodate GCs.

To help address those gaps, Google supported the GCTA in establishing the Registry Acceleration Fund. The fund awarded grants to five of the largest organizations that operate registries, which collectively issue or track 4,000 TWh of certificates in over 70+ countries. As of today, one of these organizations has met their technical milestones that would allow them to transfer, verify, and retire GCs. The remaining four organizations are expected to finish in early 2027. This will add critical functionality needed for these instruments to scale, including standardization of the hourly data and traceability to one clear owner.

3. GCs are driving real value.

Despite the GC market’s nascency, its potential benefits are moving from academic research concepts towards demonstrating real impact. For example, in a recent GCTA white paper, clean energy developers and asset operators shared real-life perspectives on granular matching. These developers explained that pricing signals from GCs can help them maximize existing energy assets in the near-term, while helping them make crucial decisions about project siting and technology diversification in the longer term.

In addition, Google, esVolta, Quintrace, and LevelTen helped prove a new revenue stream for battery energy storage system operators. We partnered to pilot the first GCs for storage systems, shifting solar generation to match our targeted demand hours. This could not have happened without hourly tracking and verification via GCs.

Hear more firsthand accounts of the benefits of GCs to developers, energy asset owners, and the grid in our new video.

In addition to the maturing global ecosystem, we’ve also continued to evolve our use of GCs to help manage Google’s emissions. We’ll always prioritize applying new, long-term clean energy agreements, and the underlying hourly GCs, first.

Even with a large clean energy portfolio, the sun doesn’t always shine and the wind doesn’t always blow exactly when we need it to. Marketplace GCs help fill those gaps. At the same time, our purchases help build a stronger market where GCs can be bought and sold quickly, easily, and in large quantities — creating clearer price signals and providing granular options for growing numbers of buyers.

We used a smaller amount of marketplace GCs alongside a much larger amount of clean energy agreements to help lower our Scope 2 market-based emissions by 3% from 2024 to 2025, despite a 37% electricity load increase. We will include a limited amount of marketplace GCs in our 24/7 CFE performance in the future.

Looking ahead, these tools will become even more important to develop. The recently released net zero standard of the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) will require reporting on hourly matching performance for large energy users, and the GHG Protocol (GHGP) is evaluating the introduction of hourly emissions reporting. We will continue to work on developing and advancing GCs — not just for our own efforts, but to ensure others can use these tools to build a better energy system.

Small businesses, big results: How teams scale with AI

From faster sales replies to easier employee onboarding, explore easy ways to cut hours of manual work in Google Workspace — plus, free courses you can take today.

Yulie Kwon Kim

VP, Product, Google Workspace

We are integrating Gemini into Google Workspace to help your small business manage logistics, training, and marketing tasks more efficiently. These tools allow you to draft documents, organize data, and respond to inquiries faster so you can focus on growing your brand. Visit our Google Workspace AI resources page to explore these features and access training courses that help you get started with AI today.

Behind almost every small business is a small team wearing every hat at once: running sales, marketing, and logistics on the shop floor — or on the go. When time and energy run short, scaling the business can seem like an impossible stretch. But driving big results shouldn’t require a big team or expensive software. With Google Workspace, AI is built into the apps you use every day, giving you an extra set of hands right where you work.

Here’s how four small businesses across the country use Google Workspace with Gemini to get busywork out of the way and get back to what matters most.

Bay Area Kids Rentals

When Tayo Lanlehin, a mom in Oakland, California, couldn’t find stylish, modern play equipment for her son’s first birthday party, she started Bay Area Kids Rentals. Logistics management is a huge part of her business, from loading delivery trucks to setting up events. Today, she uses Gemini in Gmail to help her be more efficient. She gets a daily brief of to-dos, pulls pricing from past files, and replies to inquiries in minutes instead of days. That speed has helped her close over 50% of incoming leads, double her revenue, and still make it home for dinner with her family.

Anderson Foundries

In Webster, South Dakota, husband-and-wife co-founders Kory and Ali Anderson are keeping 5,000-year-old metal casting techniques alive at Anderson Foundries. With veteran craftsmen retiring, Kory and Ali used Gemini Notebook to turn technical manuals into interactive training resources for new hires and apprentices. Beyond teaching the next generation, they use Gemini in Google Docs to draft complex quality manuals that keep their business compliant, a task that usually requires a specialized consultant. By drafting them with Gemini in-house, the team saves thousands of dollars and keeps its focus on the foundry floor.

Sourmilk

In 2025, when Elan Halpern’s homemade yogurt experiments outgrew her kitchen, she and her co-founder, Kiki Couchman, launched their probiotic Greek yogurt brand, Sourmilk. Often running the two-person business from their delivery bikes in New York City, they use Gemini in Google Sheets to help create production models and Gemini in Gmail to triage hundreds of email replies in minutes. With a little help from Gemini, the duo has been able to operate like a 10-person team and scale into more than 100 grocery stores within the brand’s first year.

Curious Elixirs

In New York’s Hudson Valley, former bar owner JW Wiseman and his team at Curious Elixirs have spent 11 years crafting booze-free, adaptogen-infused cocktails. Constantly jumping between the flavor lab, marketing, and operations, team members use Gemini in Google Docs to brainstorm marketing campaigns in their signature brand voice. They also rely on Gemini to generate styled product photos and source high-quality ingredient suppliers to keep production running smoothly.

AI for your business

You don’t need a massive budget or dozens of tools to put AI to work. These resources will help you get started.

• Google Workspace AI tools: Explore how built-in AI across Gmail, Google Docs, Sheets, Meet, and more can help your team save time on everyday tasks.

• Grow with Google AI training: Access Grow with Google resources that will help you reach more customers and streamline your work.

• Google AI Essentials course: Learn on your own schedule in courses taught by Google AI experts on using AI for daily tasks — no experience required.

• Free live workshops: Connect with a Grow with Google Coach or attend a virtual training for hands-on guidance.

items.summary: Build interactive 720p worlds with Genie 4 on the Google Gemini API. Generate coherent environments with native audio and real-time controls. Get started.
items.body:
Genie 4 is now available on the Gemini API.

Nov 19, 2026

Following yesterday's Genie 4 launch, Genie 4 is now available for developers through the Gemini API (via the Interactions API) and Google AI Studio.

Starting from a text prompt, a reference image, or both, developers can experiment with generating continuous 720p worlds at 24fps with synchronized native audio — from ambient soundscapes and sound effects to character dialogue. Using real-time keyboard controls alongside live text prompts, you can navigate environments and change weather, lighting, objects, or events on the fly. Gemini reasoning keeps the world state consistent and coherent throughout.

Whether you’re prototyping interactive experiences, visualizing designs for spatial concepts, or training robotics and AI agents, Genie 4 opens up a blank canvas for you to test ideas and define new possibilities. As a reminder every output includes imperceptible SynthID watermarking.

Try the interactive canvas and starter apps in Google AI Studio. Review pricing details and explore the Gemini API documentation to begin building.

items.summary: Improve your Google Ads performance with expert A/B testing strategies. Master AI Max experiments and Smart Bidding with our latest guide. Listen now.
items.body:
Google Ads

Build strategic A/B tests to grow your ad performance.

Nov 19, 2026

In an era of rapid AI innovation, experimentation can serve as a strategic compass. In the latest episode of Ads Decoded, Ads Product Liaison Ginny Marvin sits down with product leads Sagar Shah and Al Nevarez to explore how A/B testing validates AI Max features, budget shifts, and Smart Bidding strategies.

Three key rules to guide your testing:

• Start with templated setups: Pre-built templates isolate single variables, split traffic 50/50, and minimize setup errors for cleaner data.

• Focus on business outcomes: Measure qualified conversions rather than shallow proxies, and give tests four to six weeks to account for conversion lag.

• Match confidence to decision scope: An 80% confidence interval works well for directional tweaks. Reserve 95% certainty for major structural overhauls.

Explore the Experiments tab in Google Ads, test with confidence, and let data prove the value before scaling.
